title: Identification and Authentication Failures
description: Jotunheim demonstrates session fixation vulnerabilities through a giant fortress authentication system that accepts client-provided session IDs.
theme: Norse realm of giants - representing oversized trust in client inputs

endpoints.description: Login endpoint that accepts client-provided session IDs
Exposes session information including whether session was client-fixed
Returns flag if authenticated with admin role

vulnerabilities.description: The authentication system accepts session IDs from the client during login. An attacker can provide a known session ID, have an admin log in with it, then reuse that session to gain admin access.
vulnerabilities.impact: Session hijacking, unauthorized access to admin accounts, privilege escalation, account takeover
exploit_steps: Generate a valid session ID format (e.g., 'attack-session-12345')
Send login request with attacker-controlled sessionId in body
System creates session with the provided ID
Wait for admin to log in (or social engineer admin to use the fixed session)
Reuse the known session ID to access admin-only endpoints
Access /api/fortress-status with admin session to retrieve flag
exploit_indicators: sessionId parameter in login request body
Warning message: 'Session ID was provided by client'
Reuse of session ID across different connections
vulnerabilities.remediation: Always generate session IDs server-side using cryptographically secure random generators. Never accept session identifiers from clients. Regenerate session IDs after authentication. Implement session binding to IP/User-Agent. Use secure session management frameworks.

flags.retrieval_method: Exploit session fixation to gain admin access, then access /api/fortress-status

learning_objectives: Learn why client-provided session IDs are dangerous

scanner_test_cases.name: Verify session ID is returned in response
Test admin access with fixed session
